newsitem.title: USA: SEC says sees fall in fed court class action suits.
newsitem.headline: SEC says sees fall in fed court class action suits.

text.p: The number of companies sued in securities class actions in federal court dropped for the year following passage of a litigation reform measure, while the number of such suits in state courts has risen, the Securities and Exchange Commission said in a study released Wednesday.

The report submitted to the White House, was prepared by the SEC at President Clinton's request after passage of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, a law designed to curb certain lawsuits.
Despite the agency's findings, Levitt emphasized it is too soon to tell what impact the litigation reform has had.

"The commission endorses the ultimate conclusion of the report: it is too early to assess with confidence many important effects of the Reform Act and therefore, on this basis, it is premature to propose legislative changes," Levitt wrote to President Clinton in an April 15 letter.
Levitt said he would continue monitor the issue.

"If we find substantial evidence of a negative impact on investor protection, or that the purpose of a particular parovision is being frustrated, we will report back to you and recommend appropriate action," he said.
SEC commissioner Steven Wallman expressed concerns about the agency's method of research, faulting it for relying mostly on a review of cases.
"Consequently, I cannot support the conclusion that no further legislative change is needed at this time," Wallman said in a statement released Wednesday.

The Uniform Standards Coalition, a group that represents high-tech companies, venture capitalists, securities firms and the accounting profession, said Wednesday that "evidence is strong that lawyers who specialize in securities class action suits are trying to do an end run around a new law" enacted to guard against abusive suits.
In 1995, Congres passed a law that aims to curb the filing of abusive class actions in federal court and to encourage companies to give more information to investors.

"Unfortunately, neither of these changes is working as intended because some attorneys are thwarting the will of Congress by taking meritless securities class actions to state courts," the coalition said. "The SEC, from its vantage point in Washington, is wrong to suggest there is not enough evidence to warrant legislation to fix this problem."
The group's response follows a letter last week from the leaders of 181 high-technology companies asking Congress to enact new legislation that would be more effective than the 1995 reform measure.
Senator Pete Domenici, a Republican from New Mexico who was a sponsor of the 1995 law, endorsed this industry group's latest effort.
"Unfortunately, diclosure continues to be chilled by the threat of state securities class actions. This loophole in the law must be closed," the lawmaker said.
